SFU
Self-supervised confidence-aware denoising imputation of genomic data
Mehdi Foroozandeh, Abdul Rahman Diab, and Maxwell Libbrecht
Simon Fraser University, Department of Computing Science
mehdiforoozandeh.github.io/CANDI

The problem

Epigenomic data form a three-dimensional tensor across assays, cell types and genomic positions, with tens to hundreds of assays and thousands of cell types. Due to the high cost and complexity of profiling every possible assay in all relevant cell and tissue types, this tensor is sparse: most experiments were never performed. Epigenome imputation methods aim to predict these missing experiments [1].

CANDI

Confidence-Aware Neural Denoising Imputer [2] is a self-supervised deep learning method for epigenome imputation and denoising. It takes raw read counts, DNA sequence and experimental covariates, and outputs probability distributions over counts, signal and peaks. Conditioning on metadata rather than cell-type embeddings enables zero-shot generalization to unseen cell types.

Key findings

  • CANDI ranks 1st of 26 on the ENCODE Imputation Challenge.
  • CANDI provides calibrated uncertainty estimates.
  • CANDI's imputed signals and latent space predict gene expression.

CANDI schematic workflow

Top: for each 30 kb locus, CANDI takes observed read counts with the ChIP-seq control, four covariates per assay and the DNA sequence; grey assays were never measured, yellow ones are masked. Bottom: each output is a probability distribution, here a mean and 95% interval per assay; window by window, they fill every missing thread of the tensor.
